title: Orthodontic Referral
description: When and how to refer for orthodontic assessment — BOS guidance and Greater Manchester NHS e-referral guidance

workflows.title: When to refer in the deciduous dentition
workflows.overview:
## 1. Default position

Most children do **not** need an orthodontic referral while still in the deciduous dentition. The default is to wait until the permanent teeth are first established.

Referral at this stage is reserved for problems that need either multidisciplinary planning from infancy or skeletal management before any further development.

## 2. Refer if any of these are present

### Cleft and craniofacial
- Cleft lip and/or palate
- Other craniofacial anomalies

### Severe skeletal disproportion
- Severe maxillary/mandibular disproportion **with parental concern**
- If the parents are not concerned, it is acceptable to **wait until the mixed dentition stage**

## 3. If none of the above apply

Reassure and review. Plan to reassess at the mixed dentition stage, around the time the permanent incisors and first molars erupt.

workflows.title: When to refer in the mixed dentition
workflows.overview:
## 1. Why timing matters here

The mixed dentition is the window where many problems can be **intercepted** before they become harder to treat in the permanent dentition. Some interventions (functional appliances, eruption-guidance, cross-bite correction) work best while growth and tooth eruption are still ongoing.

Referral is therefore indication-driven, not age-driven.

## 2. Skeletal and growth-related problems

- **Anterior or posterior crossbites** with associated **mandibular displacement**
- **Class III** malocclusion in the mixed dentition
- **Class II/I** malocclusion with an underlying **skeletal II pattern** — refer **without delay** as the child enters the pubertal growth spurt, because most functional appliances are easiest to wear once the upper first premolars are fully erupted

## 3. Eruption and dental development problems

- **Asymmetry** in the pattern of tooth eruption (especially upper central incisors)
- **Lack of palpable canine bulges** buccally at **10–12 years** — indicates possible palatal impaction
- **Submerged deciduous molars**
- **Impacted first permanent molars**
- **Hypodontia** (missing teeth) and **supernumerary teeth**

## 4. Tooth-prognosis problems

- **Severely hypoplastic or carious first permanent molars** of poor long-term prognosis (timing of extraction matters for the rest of the bite)

## 5. Crowding and soft-tissue consequences

- **Severe crowding of incisors**
- **Periodontal problems caused by severely ectopic tooth position**

## 6. If none of the above are present

Defer referral until the permanent dentition is established and reassess.

workflows.title: When to refer in the permanent dentition
workflows.overview:
## 1. Default rule

Once the permanent teeth are established, **all other malocclusions** that warrant treatment can be referred. This is the standard window for orthodontic referral.

## 2. Practical timing notes

- The majority of orthodontic treatment can commence in the **late mixed / early permanent dentition**
- Refer based on **clinical findings**, not as a tactic to skip waiting lists — early-but-unjustified referrals will be returned
- Aim to refer **before the patient is 17 years old** so they have time to move through the waiting list
- If referring after age 17, document the **reason for the delay**

## 3. Pre-referral readiness check

Before submitting any referral, make sure the patient is ready for treatment:

1. **Motivation** — patient is committed to wearing the appliance
2. **Dental fitness** — no active caries lesions
3. **Oral hygiene** — good to excellent plaque control
4. **Realistic expectations** — patient and parents know they may not be eligible for NHS treatment
5. **Counselling** — discussed nature, duration, discomfort and commitment of orthodontic treatment

Patients with poor oral hygiene or active caries should **not** be referred until they have demonstrated appropriate plaque control and motivation.

## 4. Caries-risk add-on

Orthodontic patients are considered at increased caries risk. Apply *Delivering Better Oral Health* preventive advice and consider:

- **2800 ppm** fluoride toothpaste, or
- **5000 ppm** for older children

firstPrinciples.title: Referral timing follows dental development, not chronological age
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Orthodontic problems present in different windows depending on when the relevant teeth erupt. Referral timing is driven by what is biologically present, not by birthdays.
firstPrinciples.body:
## Match the referral to the dentition stage

The BOS guidance frames referral timing around three stages: deciduous, mixed, and permanent dentition. Most patients can be referred when the permanent teeth are first established [1]. The exceptions exist precisely because the underlying problem can only be addressed while specific teeth or growth processes are still in play.

## Implication for practice

When a parent asks if a child is "too young" or "too old", the answer is rarely about age alone. It is about whether the relevant teeth have erupted, whether the relevant growth is still available, and whether the malocclusion is one that benefits from interception now. Manchester reinforces this from the other direction: patients referred too early in an attempt to circumvent waiting lists will be sent back to the referring practitioner [2].

citations.quote: Most patients can be referred when the permanent teeth are first established.
citations.source: BOS Guidance, When Should I Refer for an Orthodontic Assessment?

citations.quote: Patients should be referred based on the clinical findings and not referred early in an attempt to circumvent the long waiting lists. Patients referred too early will be sent back to the referring practitioner.
citations.source: Greater Manchester NHS Orthodontic E-referral Guidance, p.1

firstPrinciples.title: Functional appliances depend on the pubertal growth spurt
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Skeletal Class II correction relies on biological growth potential. Once growth slows, the same appliance produces mostly dental change rather than skeletal change.
firstPrinciples.body:
## Why timing is non-negotiable for skeletal II patients

Functional appliances exploit residual mandibular growth to correct a skeletal Class II pattern. The window where they work best is the pubertal growth spurt, and they are physically easiest to wear once the upper first premolars are fully erupted [1]. Refer too late and the skeletal lever is gone; refer too early and the appliance does not fit.

## Implication for practice

A child with a skeletal Class II/I malocclusion entering puberty should be seen without delay. This is one of the few BOS indications where the words "without delay" appear, and it sits in the mixed dentition list rather than the permanent dentition list for exactly this reason.

citations.quote: Class II/I malocclusion where there is an underlying skeletal II pattern. Most functional appliances are easiest to wear when the upper first premolars are fully erupted. Such a patient entering his or her pubertal growth spurt should be seen without delay

firstPrinciples.title: Palpable canine bulges between 10 and 12 years are a screening test
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Maxillary canines have the longest, most tortuous eruption path of any permanent tooth. Their position can be inferred clinically before any radiograph.
firstPrinciples.body:
## A simple chairside test

By 10 to 12 years of age, the buccal canine bulge should be palpable in a child whose canines are erupting normally. If it is not palpable, the canine is suspect for palatal impaction [1]. The Manchester form makes the same screening test operational by triggering parallax radiographs at this age if the canine cannot be felt buccally or in the line of the arch [2].

## Implication for practice

Palpating the canine region at every routine paediatric exam between 10 and 12 is a free, fast intercept. Catching a palatally displaced canine early opens up options like extraction of the deciduous canine to redirect eruption, before the permanent canine becomes truly impacted and resorbs the lateral incisor root.

citations.quote: Lack of palpable canine bulges buccally at 10-12 years of age indicating palatal impaction
Age 10+yrs if not palpable buccally/ line or arch - take parallax radiographs
citations.source: Greater Manchester NHS Orthodontic E-referral Guidance, p.4

firstPrinciples.title: Crossbites with mandibular displacement are a development concern, not just an occlusal one
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: When the bite forces the mandible to shift to find intercuspation, the dentition develops around the displaced position. Left untreated, asymmetric growth can follow.
firstPrinciples.body:
## Why displacement matters

BOS singles out anterior or posterior crossbites with associated mandibular displacement as an indication to refer in the mixed dentition [1]. Manchester records the same feature in detail: posterior crossbites are graded by whether the displacement between retruded contact and intercuspal position is greater than or less than 1 mm [2].

## Implication for practice

A crossbite without displacement may be cosmetic; a crossbite with a displacement is functional and progressive. Picking up the displacement at routine exam and referring in the mixed dentition allows simple interception (e.g. a URA) before the asymmetry becomes embedded in the developing skeletal pattern.

citations.quote: Anterior or posterior crossbites with associated mandibular displacement
Posterior With RCP-ICP displacement >1mm / With RCP-ICP displacement <1mm
citations.source: Greater Manchester NHS Orthodontic E-referral Guidance, p.5

workflows.title: IOTN/MOCDO assessment for NHS eligibility
workflows.overview:
## 1. Why this exists

NHS orthodontic care is rationed by the **Index of Orthodontic Treatment Need (IOTN)**. The Greater Manchester e-referral form uses the **MOCDO method** to capture the features that determine the IOTN grade and decide whether the case meets the threshold for NHS treatment, and whether it should sit in primary or secondary care.

The online form has a built-in **algorithm** that directs the referral to secondary care only if the severity reaches hospital-based thresholds.

## 2. The MOCDO mnemonic

Record, in order:

1. **M** — **Missing teeth**: hypodontia, impactions, unerupted teeth out of normal sequence (NOT 8s)
2. **O** — **Overjet**: positive and negative measurements in mm
3. **C** — **Crossbites**: anterior (number of incisors) and posterior, with or without RCP–ICP displacement
4. **D** — **Displacements of contact points** (crowding)
5. **O** — **Overbite**: deep bites (with or without trauma), anterior open bites, or lateral open bites > 2 mm

Then capture **Additional features**: submerged deciduous teeth, supernumerary teeth, etc.

## 3. Thresholds that drive eligibility (form values)

### Missing teeth
- More than one tooth absent per quadrant (not 8s) — IOPA/DPT required
- Only one tooth missing per quadrant (not 8s) — IOPA/DPT required
- Unerupted maxillary central incisor at > 8 yrs — IOPA required

### Canines
- Age **under 10 yrs**
- Age **10+ yrs** if not palpable buccally / line of arch — take **parallax** radiographs
- Buccally placed or in line of arch with sufficient space
- Buccally placed or in line of arch with **< 4 mm** space
- Palatally placed

### Overjet
- **> 9 mm** at age 10+
- **> 9 mm** under age 10
- **6–9 mm** at age 11+
- **6–9 mm** under age 11
- **< 6 mm** any age

### Reverse overjet
- **1–3.5 mm** age < 18
- **> 3.5 mm** age < 18

### Crossbite
- Anterior: 1–2 incisors in crossbite, or 3–4 incisors
- Posterior: with RCP–ICP displacement **> 1 mm** or **< 1 mm**

### Crowding (displacement)
- More than four deciduous molars still present
- Four or fewer with: marked crowding/irregularity; mild crowding with marked aesthetic detriment; mild crowding with little aesthetic detriment; severe spacing with marked aesthetic detriment

### Open and overbites
- Lateral or anterior open bite **2–4 mm**
- Lateral or anterior open bite **> 4 mm**
- Overbite **complete and potentially traumatic**

## 4. Tertiary-care triggers

Before the MOCDO section, declare any of:

- Cleft lip and/or palate
- Craniofacial syndrome
- Other complex or congenital medical conditions (under 18s only)

These route the case via tertiary/multidisciplinary services.

## 5. Adults (> 18) special rule

- Patients **over 18** with **routine** malocclusions that do not need hospital care will **not** be accepted for NHS referral
- Only **complex malocclusions requiring multidisciplinary input** are accepted into the hospital service for over-18s
- Even when routed via *“problems likely to need specialist multidisciplinary input”*, cases must still meet **IOTN DHC ≥ 3 with aesthetic component > 6**, and will be screened by a Consultant

workflows.title: Greater Manchester NHS e-referral process (filling the form)
workflows.overview:
## 1. Where to start

All NHS orthodontic referrals in Greater Manchester are managed through the online **Orthodontic Assessment and Treatment Interactive Form** at **http://www.dental-referrals.org**.

Log in and select *Orthodontic Assessment and Treatment Interactive Form*.

## 2. Patient details

Complete patient demographics, **including GMP details**.

For patients **over 18**, the form first asks for the specific reason for **multidisciplinary care** before continuing.

## 3. Clinical information

- Select either **opinion / treatment if appropriate**, or **transfer case** if patient already in appliances
- Complete medical history
- Confirm: motivation, dental fitness, oral hygiene, NHS eligibility counselling, previous orthodontic treatment

## 4. Presenting problem (MOCDO)

Identify the **main** presenting problem, then tick all MOCDO boxes that apply (Missing, Overjet, Crossbites, Displacements/Crowding, Overbite/Openbite).

Attach radiographs where the form requires them (IOPA/DPT for hypodontia, IOPA for unerupted upper centrals, parallax for unpalpable canines).

## 5. Additional features

Tick if appropriate: submerged deciduous teeth, supernumeraries, problems likely to require hospital assessment, other (e.g. assessment of 6s, other impactions). Provide details when asked.

## 6. Referral priority

Default is **routine**. Mark **urgent** only if one of these applies:

1. Unerupted maxillary central incisor markedly delayed (IOPA required)
2. Impacted permanent canines placing incisor roots at risk (radiograph required)
3. Significant Class II skeletal discrepancy with overjet > 9 mm approaching age 13
4. Patient needing opinion before GA extraction of an acutely symptomatic first molar

If urgency cannot be justified, the patient is placed back on the routine list.

## 7. Provider and uploads

- Select preferred provider, or **leave blank** for closest to patient
- Upload supporting materials (radiographs, study models, photos)
- The algorithm decides primary vs secondary care from the data entered

## 8. Submit

On submission you receive an **acknowledgement and a URN** to track the referral. Available providers are then identified based on the clinical information.

## 9. Out-of-region transfers

- NHS transfer cases are **likely to be accepted from outside** the region
- Transfers **within** Greater Manchester will **not** be considered

firstPrinciples.title: IOTN exists to ration finite NHS treatment capacity
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Orthodontic resources are limited and demand outstrips supply. An objective index lets the system prioritise need over want.
firstPrinciples.body:
## What IOTN does

The Index of Orthodontic Treatment Need grades a malocclusion against a defined set of features so that NHS care can be targeted at cases that genuinely warrant it. The Manchester e-referral system encodes this directly: a built-in algorithm only directs referrals to secondary care if the severity of the malocclusion reaches hospital-based thresholds [1].

## Implication for practice

MOCDO (Missing teeth, Overjet, Crossbites, Displacements, Overbite) is the data-collection scaffold that produces the IOTN grade [2]. Recording these features carefully on referral is not bureaucracy — it is what determines whether the patient is offered NHS treatment at all, and whether they are seen in primary or hospital care.

citations.source: Greater Manchester NHS Orthodontic E-referral Guidance, p.1

citations.quote: Clinically, the information required is based on the MOCDO method of assessment related to the index of orthodontic treatment need (IOTN).
citations.source: Greater Manchester NHS Orthodontic E-referral Guidance, p.1

firstPrinciples.title: Adult NHS orthodontic eligibility is restricted to multidisciplinary cases
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Adult demand for cosmetic orthodontics is enormous, while NHS capacity is finite. Eligibility narrows sharply at 18 to keep resources for patients who cannot be treated otherwise.
firstPrinciples.body:
## What changes at 18

For over-18s, only complex malocclusions requiring multidisciplinary input are accepted into the hospital service [1]. Patients over 18 with routine malocclusions not requiring hospital care will not be accepted for NHS referral [2]. Even when routed via the multidisciplinary pathway, cases must still meet IOTN DHC at least 3 with an aesthetic component greater than 6, and are screened by a Consultant [3].

## Implication for practice

When counselling adult patients, set expectations early. Routine adult crowding or mild Class II is private-care territory in Greater Manchester. Reserve the NHS pathway for genuine restorative-orthodontic, surgical-orthodontic, or special-care cases, with sufficient information attached to justify the route.

firstPrinciples.title: Fixed appliances increase caries risk; oral hygiene must be sorted before referral
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Brackets and archwires create plaque-retentive niches that the patient cannot easily access. A motivated, plaque-controlled patient is the precondition for safe treatment.
firstPrinciples.body:
## Why pre-treatment hygiene matters

Orthodontic patients are considered at increased risk for caries, and Manchester explicitly invokes Delivering Better Oral Health for preventive advice [1]. The recommended preventive add-ons for these patients are 2800 ppm fluoride toothpaste, or 5000 ppm for older children [1].

## Implication for practice

A patient with poor oral hygiene or active caries lesions should not be referred until they demonstrate appropriate plaque control and motivation [2]. Sending a high-risk patient straight into fixed appliances effectively guarantees decalcification and white-spot lesions around every bracket. The pre-referral hygiene phase is part of the treatment, not a delay to it.

citations.quote: Orthodontic patients should be considered at risk for caries and practitioners should consider Delivering Better Oral Health when prescribing preventative advice and therapies. The use of high fluoride toothpaste may be indicated (2800ppm or for older children 5000ppm).

firstPrinciples.title: Treatment success depends on patient commitment as much as biology
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Orthodontic appliances only work if the patient wears them and keeps them clean. Motivation is a clinical variable, not a soft one.
firstPrinciples.body:
## Commitment as eligibility

The Manchester referral form opens its clinical section by asking whether the patient is motivated to undergo orthodontic treatment, whether they are dentally fit, and whether oral hygiene is good to excellent [1]. The guidance reinforces this with a plain warning: orthodontic treatment is time-consuming, sometimes uncomfortable, and requires commitment from patient and family [2].

## Implication for practice

The pre-referral conversation is not a formality. Discuss the duration, the wear schedule, the discomfort, and the dietary and hygiene constraints before submitting the referral. A patient who declines that conversation, or who cannot demonstrate plaque control, is not yet ready, regardless of how high their IOTN grade is.
